# 1. Project overview

This analysis examines spatial autocorrelation in the E-food Desert Index (EFDI) across 2,365 Lower Layer Super Output Areas (LSOAs) in the West Midlands, England.

Four spatial weighting methods are constructed and compared:

1. Queen contiguity
2. K-nearest neighbours (KNN6)
3. Distance band (6 km)
4. Inverse distance (6 km, power 1)

The analysis examines neighbour structures, spatial weights, Global Moran's I, Local Moran's I, spatial patterns and descriptive statistics.

**Input:** `efdi_wm_clean.gpkg`

**Identifier:** `lsoa01cd`

**Geometry column:** `geom`

**Analysis CRS:** EPSG:27700 — OSGB36 / British National Grid.

# 2. Install and load packages

```{r packages, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
packages <- c(
  "sf",
  "spdep",
  "spatialreg",
  "dplyr",
  "ggplot2",
  "tidyr",
  "purrr",
  "knitr"
)

missing_packages <- packages[
  !packages %in% rownames(installed.packages())
]

if (length(missing_packages) > 0) {
  install.packages(missing_packages)
}

library(sf)
library(spdep)
library(spatialreg)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(knitr)

set.seed(12345)

# Show package versions
packageVersion("sf")
packageVersion("spdep")
packageVersion("spatialreg")
```

# 3. Read the West Midlands dataset

```{r read-data}
# Project directory
project_dir <- "D:/Spatial Data Analysis"

# Input GeoPackage
data_path <- file.path(
  project_dir,
  "efdi_wm_clean.gpkg"
)

# Confirm file exists
if (!file.exists(data_path)) {
  stop("The GeoPackage file could not be found.")
}

# Read spatial data
food <- st_read(
  data_path,
  quiet = TRUE
)

# Inspect data
head(food)

# Number of observations
nrow(food)

# Column names
names(food)

# Geometry column name
attr(food, "sf_column")

# Data structure
str(food)

# Geometry type
unique(st_geometry_type(food))

# CRS
st_crs(food)
```

# 4. Prepare the analytical dataset

The active geometry column in this GeoPackage is `geom`, not `geometry`. The code below uses `st_geometry()` so that the spatial operations work with the active geometry column.

```{r prepare-data}
# Check original CRS
st_crs(food)

# Transform to British National Grid if necessary
if (st_crs(food)$epsg != 27700) {
  food <- st_transform(food, 27700)
}

# Check required columns
required_fields <- c(
  "lsoa01cd",
  "efdi",
  "geom"
)

missing_fields <- setdiff(
  required_fields,
  names(food)
)

if (length(missing_fields) > 0) {
  stop(
    paste(
      "Missing required fields:",
      paste(missing_fields, collapse = ", ")
    )
  )
}

# Retain observations with EFDI values
food_analysis <- food %>%
  filter(!is.na(efdi))

# Remove empty geometries using the active geometry
food_analysis <- food_analysis[
  !st_is_empty(st_geometry(food_analysis)),
]

# Check unique LSOA identifiers
stopifnot(
  !anyDuplicated(food_analysis$lsoa01cd)
)

# Check and repair invalid geometries
invalid <- !st_is_valid(food_analysis)

if (any(invalid)) {
  food_analysis <- st_make_valid(food_analysis)
}

# Verify analytical dataset
cat("Observations:", nrow(food_analysis), "\n")
cat("Missing EFDI:", sum(is.na(food_analysis$efdi)), "\n")
cat("Empty geometries:",
    sum(st_is_empty(st_geometry(food_analysis))), "\n")
cat("Invalid geometries:",
    sum(!st_is_valid(food_analysis)), "\n")
cat("CRS:", st_crs(food_analysis)$epsg, "\n")

# Inspect result
head(food_analysis)
```

# 5. Create representative points

Queen contiguity uses polygon boundaries. KNN and distance-based weights use representative locations.

A representative point is generated inside each LSOA using `st_point_on_surface()`.

```{r representative-points}
# Generate one point inside each LSOA
representative_points <- st_point_on_surface(
  food_analysis
)

# Extract coordinates
coords <- st_coordinates(
  representative_points
)

# Check coordinates
head(coords)

# Number of points
nrow(coords)

# Confirm CRS
st_crs(representative_points)
```

The coordinate system is EPSG:27700, so distances are measured in metres.

# 6. Queen contiguity weights

Queen contiguity defines two LSOAs as neighbours when their polygons share an edge or a corner.

```{r queen-weights}
nb_queen <- poly2nb(
  food_analysis,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = food_analysis$lsoa01cd
)

# Inspect neighbour structure
summary(nb_queen)

# Number of neighbours per LSOA
queen_counts <- card(nb_queen)

# Descriptive statistics
summary(queen_counts)

# Islands
sum(queen_counts == 0)

# Create row-standardised weights
lw_queen <- nb2listw(
  nb_queen,
  style = "W",
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

# Inspect listw object
summary(lw_queen)

str(lw_queen, max.level = 2)
```

# 7. K-nearest neighbours (KNN6)

KNN6 assigns six nearest representative points to every LSOA.

Unlike Queen contiguity, the areas do not have to share a boundary.

```{r knn6-weights}
# Identify six nearest neighbours
knn_result <- knearneigh(
  coords,
  k = 6,
  longlat = FALSE
)

# Convert to neighbour list
nb_knn6 <- knn2nb(
  knn_result,
  row.names = food_analysis$lsoa01cd
)

# Inspect neighbour structure
summary(nb_knn6)

# Number of neighbours
knn_counts <- card(nb_knn6)

# Descriptive statistics
summary(knn_counts)

# Create row-standardised weights
lw_knn6 <- nb2listw(
  nb_knn6,
  style = "W",
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

# Inspect listw object
summary(lw_knn6)

str(lw_knn6, max.level = 2)
```

# 8. Distance-band weights (6 km)

The distance-band method connects LSOAs whose representative points are within 6,000 metres of one another.

```{r distance-weights}
# Create distance-band neighbours
nb_dist6 <- dnearneigh(
  coords,
  d1 = 0,
  d2 = 6000,
  row.names = food_analysis$lsoa01cd,
  longlat = FALSE
)

# Inspect neighbour structure
summary(nb_dist6)

# Number of neighbours
dist6_counts <- card(nb_dist6)

# Descriptive statistics
summary(dist6_counts)

# Check islands
sum(dist6_counts == 0)

# Create row-standardised weights
lw_dist6 <- nb2listw(
  nb_dist6,
  style = "W",
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

# Inspect listw object
summary(lw_dist6)

str(lw_dist6, max.level = 2)
```

# 9. Inverse-distance weights (6 km, power 1)

This method uses the same 6 km neighbourhood definition but gives closer LSOAs greater weights.

The inverse-distance relationship is:

\[
w_{ij} = \frac{1}{d_{ij}}
\]

where \(d_{ij}\) is the distance between representative points.

```{r inverse-distance-weights}
# Use the distance-band neighbour structure
# and the representative points to calculate inverse distances.

lw_idw6 <- nb2listwdist(
  neighbours = nb_dist6,
  x = representative_points,
  type = "idw",
  style = "W",
  alpha = 1,
  longlat = FALSE,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

# Inspect weights
summary(lw_idw6)

str(lw_idw6, max.level = 2)
```

`style = "W"` row-standardises the weights. `alpha = 1` applies inverse distance to the first power.

# 10. Organise the four neighbour and weights objects

```{r organise-weights}
# Neighbour lists
nb_objects <- list(
  Queen = nb_queen,
  KNN6 = nb_knn6,
  Distance_6km = nb_dist6,
  Inverse_Distance_6km = nb_dist6
)

# Spatial weights objects
lw_objects <- list(
  Queen = lw_queen,
  KNN6 = lw_knn6,
  Distance_6km = lw_dist6,
  Inverse_Distance_6km = lw_idw6
)

# Check all four objects
names(lw_objects)

# Confirm observation counts
sapply(lw_objects, function(x) length(x$neighbours))
```

# 11. Compare neighbour statistics

```{r weights-summary}
weights_summary <- map2_dfr(
  nb_objects,
  names(nb_objects),
  function(nb, method) {

    counts <- card(nb)

    tibble(
      Method = method,
      Observations = length(nb),
      Minimum_neighbours = min(counts),
      Maximum_neighbours = max(counts),
      Mean_neighbours = mean(counts),
      Median_neighbours = median(counts),
      Islands = sum(counts == 0)
    )
  }
)

knitr::kable(
  weights_summary,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Comparison of the four neighbour structures"
)
```

# 15. Global Moran's I — analytical inference

Global Moran's I measures the overall spatial autocorrelation of EFDI.

The four methods use the same EFDI variable and observations, but different spatial weights.

```{r global-moran-analytical}
# EFDI values
y <- food_analysis$efdi

# Analytical Global Moran's I tests
global_tests <- lapply(
  lw_objects,
  function(lw) {

    moran.test(
      y,
      lw,
      randomisation = TRUE,
      zero.policy = TRUE
    )
  }
)

# Extract results
global_summary <- map2_dfr(
  global_tests,
  names(global_tests),
  function(test, method) {

    tibble(
      Method = method,
      Moran_I = as.numeric(test$estimate[1]),
      Expected_I = as.numeric(test$estimate[2]),
      Variance = as.numeric(test$estimate[3]),
      Statistic = as.numeric(test$statistic),
      P_value = test$p.value
    )
  }
)

knitr::kable(
  global_summary,
  digits = 6,
  caption = "Global Moran's I — analytical inference"
)
```

# 16. Global Moran's I — permutation inference

The permutation test compares the observed Global Moran's I with values generated by randomly reallocating EFDI values across the fixed spatial weights.

```{r global-moran-permutation}
set.seed(12345)

global_permutation <- lapply(
  lw_objects,
  function(lw) {

    moran.mc(
      y,
      lw,
      nsim = 999,
      zero.policy = TRUE
    )
  }
)

permutation_summary <- map2_dfr(
  global_permutation,
  names(global_permutation),
  function(test, method) {

    tibble(
      Method = method,
      Moran_I = as.numeric(test$statistic),
      P_value = test$p.value,
      Permutations = 999
    )
  }
)

knitr::kable(
  permutation_summary,
  digits = 6,
  caption = "Global Moran's I — permutation inference"
)
```

# 18. Local Moran's I — LISA analysis

Local Moran's I identifies local spatial clusters and spatial outliers.

The analysis calculates:

- Local Moran's I
- Expected local Moran's I
- Local variance
- Z-score
- Analytical p-value
- Spatial lag
- Quadrant classification

```{r lisa-function}
calculate_lisa <- function(data, y, lw) {

  # Local Moran's I
  lisa <- localmoran(
    y,
    lw,
    zero.policy = TRUE
  )

  # Standardised EFDI
  z <- as.numeric(scale(y))

  # Spatial lag of standardised EFDI
  lag_z <- lag.listw(
    lw,
    z,
    zero.policy = TRUE
  )

  # Quadrant classification
  quadrant <- case_when(
    z >= 0 & lag_z >= 0 ~ "High-High",
    z < 0 & lag_z < 0 ~ "Low-Low",
    z < 0 & lag_z >= 0 ~ "Low-High",
    z >= 0 & lag_z < 0 ~ "High-Low"
  )

  # Store local Moran results
  output <- data %>%
    mutate(
      local_I = lisa[, "Ii"],
      expected_local_I = lisa[, "E.Ii"],
      local_variance = lisa[, "Var.Ii"],
      local_Z = lisa[, "Z.Ii"],
      local_p = lisa[, "Pr(z != E(Ii))"],
      spatial_lag = lag_z,
      quadrant = quadrant,
      cluster = ifelse(
        local_p < 0.05,
        quadrant,
        "Not significant"
      )
    )

  output
}
```

# 19. Run Local Moran's I for all four methods

```{r lisa-four-methods}
lisa_results <- lapply(
  lw_objects,
  function(lw) {

    calculate_lisa(
      food_analysis,
      y,
      lw
    )
  }
)

names(lisa_results) <- names(lw_objects)

# Inspect Queen results
head(
  lisa_results$Queen %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    select(
      lsoa01cd,
      efdi,
      local_I,
      expected_local_I,
      local_variance,
      local_Z,
      local_p,
      quadrant,
      cluster
    )
)
```

# 20. Compare Local Moran's I cluster counts

```{r lisa-counts}
lisa_counts <- map2_dfr(
  lisa_results,
  names(lisa_results),
  function(data, method) {

    data %>%
      st_drop_geometry() %>%
      count(cluster) %>%
      mutate(Method = method)
  }
) %>%
  select(
    Method,
    cluster,
    n
  )

knitr::kable(
  lisa_counts,
  caption = "LISA cluster counts by spatial weights"
)
```

# 25. Final comparison and interpretation

The four weighting methods represent different assumptions about spatial relationships.

| Method | Neighbour definition | Main characteristic |
|---|---|---|
| Queen | Shared edge or corner | Physical polygon contiguity |
| KNN6 | Six nearest representative points | Fixed number of neighbours |
| Distance band | Representative points within 6 km | Variable number of neighbours |
| Inverse distance | Within 6 km, weighted by inverse distance | Closer locations receive greater weights |

Compare the following:

1. How the number of neighbours differs between methods.
2. Whether Global Moran's I changes between weighting methods.
3. Whether permutation tests support the same conclusion.
4. Whether High–High and Low–Low clusters occur in similar locations.
5. Whether local spatial outliers change.
6. Which weighting method best represents the spatial interaction process relevant to EFDI.

The final methodological choice should be justified by the nature of the EFDI application, not simply by selecting the method with the largest Moran's I.

# 26. Important methodological notes

- The analytical dataset contains 2,365 LSOAs with EFDI values.
- The coordinate reference system is EPSG:27700.
- The active geometry column is `geom`.
- The four methods use the same observations and EFDI variable.
- KNN6 and distance-band neighbours are based on representative points.
- Inverse-distance weights use the same 6 km neighbourhood definition and power 1.
- All four weights objects are row-standardised using style `"W"`.
- Global Moran's I analytical and permutation tests are reported separately.
- Local Moran's I in this document uses analytical p-values from `localmoran()`. These are not the same as Python's permutation-based local p-values.
- Local p-values use an unadjusted 0.05 threshold. Consider multiple-testing correction before making strong claims about individual LSOAs.
- Results should be interpreted only after successfully running the code and checking the outputs.
